articles.title: When is Apple’s next event? Dates, rumors, and what to expect
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple’s WWDC keynote may be long behind us now, but Apple’s event calendar for 2026 is far from finished. With iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and the latest Apple Intelligence and Siri updates now unveiled, attention is turning to the company’s...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple’s WWDC keynote may be long behind us now, but Apple’s event calendar for 2026 is far from finished. With iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and the latest Apple Intelligence and Siri updates now unveiled, attention is turning to the company’s next big launch.

Apple rarely confirms event dates far in advance, and there’s no guarantee an event will take place within its usual window. That leaves Apple fans – and anyone considering a new Apple device – wondering when the next Apple event will happen and what might be announced.

Luckily, Apple’s annual schedule is predictable, giving us a good idea of when the next keynote will happen – and which products are likely to launch. Based on Apple’s long-established schedule and reliable rumours, we can make informed estimates about when the next keynote is likely and which products could headline it.

From the iPhone 18 lineup and new Apple Watches to potential Mac and iPad updates, here’s everything we know about Apple’s next event and what you can expect to see. Read on for a closer look at all of the events Apple is expected to hold in 2026 and beyond, and what could launch.

When is Apple’s next event?

Apple still hasn’t made an official announcement about the date

Beginning of September (expected)

Apple has not yet announced the date of its next event, although the company has asked Apple Store staff to apply for the ” Event Support Experience Program.” Employees enter a lottery for the opportunity to assist with an Apple event scheduled for the first half of September.

Based on Apple’s typical event schedule, we expect the company’s next event to be the annual iPhone launch in September 2026.

Looking at Apple’s event history over the past several years, we predict the September event will take place during the week beginning September 7, with September 9 the most likely date because September 7 is labor day and Apple is not expected to hold an event the day after a public holiday. The event could also be pushed back to September 15 – this would avoid pre-orders falling on 9/11 (Friday, September 11) something that Apple has avoided in the past.

As in previous years, Apple is expected to livestream the event, allowing viewers around the world to watch the company unveil its latest products. One notable change this year is that the keynote is expected to be hosted by John Ternus, who is set to succeed Tim Cook as Apple’s CEO following Cook’s retirement.

Apple event calendar 2026

Apple has held two events so far in 2026, although the first was not an event in the traditional sense. On March 4, the company invited select media to hands-on “experiences” in multiple locations. In the run-up to that date, Apple also launched several products via press release, including the iPhone 17e, M4 iPad Air, and MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max, M5 MacBook Air and the MacBook Neo.

The second event was WWDC, which began with a keynote on June 8. At the WWDC keynote Apple outlined the upcoming changes to its operating systems, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Looking ahead to the fall, Apple is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, a foldable iPhone Ultra, and more at an Apple event in September.

A second, late-fall event in October or November is possible, though less certain and typically focused on Macs or iPads.

articles.title: Meta AI is now available as a more capable desktop app for Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI. Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI.

Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.

Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app.

Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Beyond chat, the sidebar includes Media, Artifacts, scheduled tasks, conversation history, and an “About Me” personalization section.

Users can switch among thinking modes, attach files, generate media, and create recurring briefings or reminders. The app also includes the ability to hide the Dock icon, allowing it to be invoked with a keyboard shortcut instead.

Meta’s recent AI push

The Mac app is the latest in a steady run of releases. In April, Meta replaced Llama with Muse Spark. A May update then expanded Meta AI with more natural voice conversations and live camera-based assistance.

July brought Muse-powered image generation to Meta AI, WhatsApp, and Instagram, although Meta quickly removed one feature that generated images from public Instagram posts. Meta AI also moved into Threads DMs for private chats.

Most recently, Meta launched Muse Code, a terminal-based AI coding agent for macOS and Linux.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

articles.title: The Scariest Thing In The Silent Hill: Townfall Gameplay Trailer Is How Scots Pay For Electricity
articles.subtitle: Konami Silent Hill: Townfall Konami has released a 19-minute-long gameplay trailer for Silent Hill: Townfall, showing off what seem to be the opening moments of the game, delving into gameplay mechanics, and hinting at story elements that left me with far...
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Konami Silent Hill: Townfall

Konami has released a 19-minute-long gameplay trailer for Silent Hill: Townfall, showing off what seem to be the opening moments of the game, delving into gameplay mechanics, and hinting at story elements that left me with far more intriguing questions than hard answers as to what this game is about.

The video starts by slowly introducing us to the fictional Scottish island of St. Amelia, as a voice tells a man named Simon that he has to set things right. In typical Silent Hill fashion, this message to Simon is vaguely menacing and everything’s covered in fog. Simon suddenly bursts out of the water, Bioshock style, and we’re off to the survival horror races.

Silent Hill: Townfall brings back the series’ staple radio, but because the game takes place in 1996, it’s not exactly a radio but rather one of those neat handheld CRTVs. Simon has to tune the TV until he gets a solid signal, then look for the building the TV displays, which is a neat way for the game to nudge you from objective to objective. The TV also has a station that acts like monster radar.

When Simon’s tuned in, he can tell if enemies are nearby and what direction they’re coming from. Later on in the demo, Simon can use objects in the environment to distract enemies and sneak by them, but if that fails there’s always the other Silent Hill staple: gun.

Once Simon finds the first location, guided by a woman exhorting him to return to her, things get interesting. The first thing I noticed is that Simon is hooked up to an IV and has a blood bag strapped to his arm. Then, when he enters the house, there’s a locked human organ container with a note taped to it like, “here bro, you need this.

” Then, just as I’m wondering what the fuck all is going on, the gameplay demo hits me with another bewildering moment. Simon is tasked with restoring power to the house.

When he locates the breaker— through typical Silent Hill actions including finding a flashlight, then finding batteries to power it— there’s a contraption that asks him to insert a prepaid electricity card before the power can start running. What?

At the beginning of the demo there are hand-painted protest signs with slogans like “This town is ours” and “We need justice. ” The presence of a prepay-by-the-watt meter suggested to me this was a town overrun by an expressly evil energy company and that’s what Simon has to put right somehow. I was wrong.

After consulting with Kotaku ‘s UK correspondent John Walker, I learned that’s a valid method some less-resourced folks in the UK use to get their power. Damn, they make y’all live like that? (She, the American, asks. )

It doesn’t sound sexy to say my biggest “what the fuck” moment watching a Silent Hill video came from learning how some Brits pay for their power, but I think Konami has done a really good job with this gameplay demo.

It doesn’t provide a flashy exposition of what to expect in the game; sure, there are your typical “gotta find the combination to this lockbox” moments, but it’s well-executed from a craft perspective.

I didn’t come away from the video hyped about beating monsters to death with a 2×4; rather, I’m excited to have been so thoroughly drawn into a world I want to understand, and left with questions I’m desperate to know the answers to.

Why is Simon strapped to an IV? What the hell is he supposed to do with that organ? If his goal is not to free the town from a rapacious energy company, what is it that he has to put right? I’ll find out when Silent Hill: Townfall releases on September 24th.

articles.title: Jungle Shot 11 Music Videos in Four Days with Apple Creator Studio
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Jungle released their fifth studio album, Sunshine. Alongside the release, Apple published a look at how the band used Apple Creator Studio to film 11 music videos in just four days, an impressive feat no matter the technology used.

The band’s toolbox included Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Pixelmator Pro to capture the series of signature one-shot take videos. According to the App Store feature on the band’s process, Logic Pro was where the entire album was produced. The app’s Varispeed feature was also used to shift the tempo of songs while maintaining pitch as they shot the videos.

Final Cut Pro’s Magnetic Mask was used to composite footage quickly. Jungle’s Tom McFarland told Apple:

Final Cut Pro is like a magic sword. There’s one shot for the track ‘Romeo II,’ where the camera accidentally caught some of the lighting rig. With five clicks, the editor was able to paint it out. It just automatically knows.

Pixelmator Pro on the iPad with an Apple Pencil and Mac enabled the band’s team to add artwork and posters to the final product, too.

But of all the quotes from the band, J Lloyd’s comment really struck a chord with me:

We didn’t have to worry about the tech. We could just focus on getting the design right. I could pick up the iPad between takes and keep sketching on Pixelmator Pro, and it all just worked.

I love apps, or I wouldn’t write about them every day, but what I love even more is the creativity they enable. Getting a glimpse of how one of my favorite bands uses some of the same tools I do was a treat.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: 5 Apple Products to Get OLED Displays
articles.subtitle: Apple plans to upgrade several iPads and Macs with OLED displays over the next three years, according to a new DigiTimes report.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple plans to upgrade several iPads and Macs with OLED displays over the next three years, according to a new DigiTimes report.

The following five devices will receive OLED displays between 2026 and 2029, according to the Taiwanese publication's industry sources:

iPad mini: 2026

MacBook Pro: Late 2026 or early 2027

iPad Air: 2027

iMac: 2028 or 2029

MacBook Air: 2028 or 2029

OLED displays have better overall image quality compared to LCD displays, thanks to richer colors and higher contrast ratio with true blacks.

All current iPhone, Apple Watch, and iPad Pro models already have OLED displays.

While the iPad Pro features so-called "Tandem OLED" technology that uses two OLED panels for increased brightness, and ProMotion support for up to a 120Hz refresh rate, the report said the iPad Air will have a single-stack OLED display and an LTPS backplane, meaning it will have lower brightness and a 60Hz refresh rate. These limitations would make sense given that the iPad Air is priced hundreds of dollars less than the iPad Pro.

It is unclear if Apple ever plans to release a Studio Display XDR with an OLED display. The monitor currently has mini-LED backlighting.

The entry-level iPad and MacBook Neo are expected to stick with LCD displays.

articles.title: Hands-On with Computer History: OpenAI’s Take on Agent Memory
articles.subtitle: Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into...
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Late yesterday, OpenAI revealed the sort of automation catnip I love: Computer History. It’s a new feature for Pro, Business, and Enterprise subscribers that creates continuity for ChatGPT and Codex by converting the actions you take on your Mac into Markdown memory files that serve as context for subsequent interactions.

The idea is that with the additional context, ChatGPT and Codex will better understand your requests, requiring you to provide less detail up front while getting better results. Anyone familiar with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and similar projects will know where this is going.

Here’s how it works.

Computer History is currently a Mac-only feature that is turned off by default, so if you want to try it, head to the Integrations section of the desktop app’s settings and toggle it on. History entries can be cleared individually, too. Before you get started, ChatGPT explains that you can pause or clear your history and manage the apps and websites that Computer History accesses at any time.

I excluded Passwords, 1Password, and Keychain Access to start and may add to that list as I use the feature more and get a better sense for the sort of information that it collects.

That opening alert also says you agree to pause Computer History during video and audio calls with others to avoid recording them without their consent. I appreciate the reminder that recording people without consent is something you shouldn’t do and is even illegal in some places, but as with the many meeting summarization tools on the market, I doubt that very many people will heed the warning and comply even though doing so is just a click of the menu bar away.

Still, I appreciate the alert up front, because turning Computer History on requires trust that the information won’t be misused by OpenAI. I’m sure that’s a bridge too far for some, but one of the most frustrating parts of using a tool like Codex is explaining yourself over and over. Every thread is like Groundhog Day for an agent, and while there are techniques that help provide continuity, making it automatic with Computer History is an exciting prospect.

If you’re intrigued by the potential, it pays to read OpenAI’s documentation and understand how the feature works. First of all, Computer History is not the same as Chronicle, a retired research preview feature that relied on taking screenshots as you worked.

In contrast, Computer History records interaction events but not screenshots, audio, or private web browsing sessions, according to OpenAI’s documentation. In practice, what that means is that as you work, ChatGPT will record your switches from app to app and what you’re doing in apps. Here’s what it’s captured as I started work on this story:

As you can see, every 10 minutes, ChatGPT creates a brief, timestamped summary of what I’ve been doing and lists the apps I’ve used by their icons. If I hover over an entry, I can immediately delete it or open the source file in the Finder for more detail on the information that ChatGPT is collecting.

Each entry in Computer History is a Markdown file with YAML front matter that includes a title, description, and list of the apps you’ve used followed by a structured memory document. Here, you’ll see a summary of what you’ve done:

The user continued writing computer history. md in Obsidian’s MacStories Vault, refining the section that explains how Computer History differs from the earlier Chronicle preview and adding a practical description of what the feature records while the user works.

The user referenced the OpenAI Learn Computer History documentation in Safari, briefly exchanged messages with Federico Viticci, checked ChatGPT/Codex settings, and then opened MacStories Images to queue a screenshot named CleanShot 2026-08-14 at 06. 08. 44@2x. png for upload. The upload was queued by the end of the segment, but no completed upload or copied Markdown image link was observed.

You’ll also find details that ChatGPT deems important and non-obvious, such as the following:

Important non-obvious context about the user MacStories Vault - Obsidian vault where the Computer History article draft was active. computer history. md - active note being drafted for the Computer History article. The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

Intelligent Home app notifications

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
“We are the spark that’ll light the fire to burn the First Order down”

Related

Like the prequel trilogy, the Star Wars sequel trilogy has often been bogged down by so much criticism that it's hard to talk about the sequels' positive qualities. A prime example is the era’s new characters, such as Rey, Finn, Poe Dameron, and Kylo Ren. Even more minor characters like Rose Tico, General Hux, Amilyn Holdo, and Jannah, have wormed their way into our hearts.

The last time we saw any of these characters on the silver screen was in 2019’s The Rise of Skywalker, but some fans might not know there’s plenty of spin-off material — books, comics, you name it — that follows the sequel characters. One of our personal favorites set in this era? The 2016 Poe Dameron comics. If you missed Poe’s adventures back then, you’re in luck: an omnibus compiling the stories of the best pilot the Resistance ever had is arriving this September.

What is the Poe Dameron Omnibus about?

The Poe Dameron Omnibus is a collection of canon adventures that follow Resistance pilot Poe Dameron, who was first introduced in 2015’s The Force Awakens and portrayed in the movies by Oscar Isaac. Poe, following in his parents’ footsteps, was a New Republic flyer who put his skills to use when General Leia Organa called on him to lead his Black Squadron on a top-secret mission.

Poe’s background wasn’t explored in depth in the sequel films, aside from the reveal in The Rise of Skywalker that he also spent some time smuggling drugs in his youth.

The comics included in the Poe Dameron Omnibus don’t go into detail about that aspect of Poe’s life, but they do touch on Poe’s childhood, his relationship with beloved astromech BB-8, and the other characters who make up the Black Squadron, such as Jessika Pava and Snap Wexley.

Each adventure featuring Poe and the Black Squadron highlights the challenges they faced before, during, and after The Force Awakens and The Last Jedi.

What comics are included in the Poe Dameron Omnibus?

There are three different comic series that make up the Poe Dameron Omnibus, which we’ve listed below:

Poe Dameron (2016) #1-31

Poe Dameron Annual #1-2

Poe Dameron 1: SaBBotage

The 31-issue Poe Dameron comic is written by Charles Soule, with art by Phil Noto and Angel Unzueta. The first issue debuted on April 6 2016, and the finale concluded on Sept. 26, 2018. Check out the first five pages below.

Image: Marvel

While largely about Poe and his Black Squadron, each issue also addresses the Resistance’s ongoing struggle against the powerful First Order. The first few issues focus on Poe and Black Squadron leading up to The Force Awakens, and the plot continues after the first sequel movie and through The Last Jedi. This means that, even if you’re not a huge Poe fan, there are plenty of cameos from characters like Rey, Finn, Leia, and Chewbacca to enjoy.

Poe Dameron Annual #1-2 is written by Robbie Thompson, with art by Nicole Virella. The two-issue series follows Poe after he disobeys a direct order from Leia Organa, leaving Poe and BB-8 stranded in First Order space. Thankfully, Poe's dealt with a lot worse in his time. The series debuted on June 27, 2017, and concluded on Aug. 29, 2018.

articles.title: Big Walk: A Good Hang with Friends
articles.subtitle: I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
I dove into Big Walk with no expectations at all. I’d seen trailers leading up to the launch and knew that it was a co-op puzzle game from House House, the makers of Untitled Goose Game, but that was about it. And because most of my gaming is done solo, I initially tuned out most of the game’s post-launch headlines. Still, Big Walk is published by Panic, which has a great track record for finding and publishing great indie games, so I decided to give it a try earlier this week. And you know what? I love it.

Big Walk is about as low-key as a puzzle game gets in the best possible way. Co-op is the only mode, so you’ll need to coordinate a time to play it with a friend or group. One person takes the lead, setting up the session and inviting the others. The process is far simpler than trying to find a time that works for everyone in your group.

As players join, you’re dropped into a space to wait for the others and explore a little. This lobby space is where you’ll learn the game’s controls, too. Big Walk supports keyboard and mouse input as well as a controller, which is what I used, playing on an M4 Max MacBook Pro.

Once you get your bearings, it’s time to exit the lobby and start exploring. That exploration is core to what Big Walk is all about. You aren’t told what to do, but there are just enough clues to push you forward, figuring out the goals on your own without too much trouble.

I played using AirPods Pro 3, and the game made great use of their mics and speakers, simulating the environments we were in. Closed spaces were echoey, and speech was distant and faint when we were separated. Sound even becomes part of the mechanic in some puzzles, such as an early one where you have to look through an open window to hear each other properly and help guide the other player’s actions.

That cooperation is the key part of the game’s loop. You may see how to solve Big Walk’s puzzles on your own, but implementing the solution will require you and a companion to work together.

The togetherness of it all extends beyond the puzzles, too. Big Walk’s environment (at least in the early stages) is mountainous with large rocks and trees that make it possible to get separated from others. Add to that day and night cycles where it’s almost impossible to see where you’re going at night without a light, and you have every incentive not to wander off on your own without a plan for how to reconnect.

I’ve played through Big Walk’s first couple of sections, and it was a blast. The puzzles were clever and challenging without being frustrating, but most of all, I enjoyed working through them with someone else. There’s no time pressure or monsters lurking around corners – just puzzles and a chance to chat.

Ultimately, that’s what makes Big Walk work. It’s a good hang built against the backdrop of a beautiful landscape and low-key, fun challenges. I highly recommend giving it a try.

Big Walk, which supports crossplay and 2–12 players, is available on the Mac App Store for $14.99. The game is also on Steam, the Switch 2, and PS5.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: PlayStation and Xbox Sales Are in Big Trouble After Massive Price Hikes
articles.subtitle: Video game console prices are up and sales are way down Related If you need another reason to hate generative AI, the technology is indirectly tanking gaming hardware sales. Industry analyst Circana just released a new report on U.S.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Video game console prices are up and sales are way down

Related

If you need another reason to hate generative AI, the technology is indirectly tanking gaming hardware sales. Industry analyst Circana just released a new report on U.S. game market trends for July 2026, and the numbers don’t look good.

“Hardware spending fell to a July low not seen since 2020,” Circana’s Mat Piscatella wrote on Bluesky. In July 2020, the game industry was in the midst of global supply chain issues caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, which made it difficult to purchase many game consoles.

In addition to game sales dropping 9% from last July, gaming hardware sales fell a whopping 29% from last year.

As for where AI comes into play, the tech industry’s rush to build AI data centers has created a shortage of RAM that's used in consumer electronics. This situation has been dubbed the “ RAM-pocalypse ” or “RAM-geddon. ” Console manufacturers have raised hardware prices significantly to cover rising component costs amid scarcity.

“Higher hardware prices driven by the RAM and component crisis have significantly impacted the selling rates of both PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, with a price hike for Nintendo Switch 2 hardware coming on September 1st, 2026,” Piscatella wrote.

July 2026 U.S. Video Game Market Highlights Thread from Circana - U.S. video game spending dropped 10% in July, to $4.5 billion, despite the debut of several hit new releases. — Mat Piscatella (@matpiscatella.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T13:05:47.456Z

July 2026 U.S. Video Game Total Spending - Mobile content was the biggest driver of the overall decline, with both Console and PC content also fell year-on-year (mobile spending provided by Sensor Tower). Hardware spending fell to a July low not seen since 2020. — Mat Piscatella (@matpiscatella.bsky.social) 2026-08-20T13:05:47.457

Each major console manufacturer has raised console prices in recent months. Sony upped the price of the base PS5 from $499.99 to $549.99 in August 2025, then increased it again this April by another $100. The console is now $649.99, $150 more than at release in 2020. Meanwhile, Microsoft’s Xbox Series X has gone through three price increases, with the Xbox Series X now going for $799.99, $300 more than at launch. The Nintendo Switch 2 is getting a $50 price hike in September.

At this point in a console generation, these systems would normally see significant price cuts, something that helps bolster player bases and drive software sales. With the ongoing RAM and component shortage undercutting this trend, it’s a bit unclear how Sony and Microsoft are going to handle the next generation of consoles.

Microsoft has made the upcoming Project Helix sound like an expensive and niche platform, while Sony president and CEO Hiroki Totoki recently made it clear that Sony hasn’t set a release date for PlayStation 6. In response to the memory chip shortage, Totoki said, “We need to take some action. Otherwise, we cannot survive in this landscape.” Needless to say, the game industry has seen better days.

articles.subtitle: Grand Theft Auto 6 GTA 6 Leak Rockstar Games On Tuesday afternoon, leaked footage of Grand Theft Auto 6 began spreading across the internet courtesy of a person or group known as Cyberleek.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Grand Theft Auto 6 GTA 6 Leak Rockstar Games

On Tuesday afternoon, leaked footage of Grand Theft Auto 6 began spreading across the internet courtesy of a person or group known as Cyberleek. Since then, Rockstar Games has remained completely radio silent across all platforms as fans continue to share and debate the gameplay leaks.

On August 20 at 10 a. m. EST, the Rockstar Games Twitter account didn’t post anything. This is a bit peculiar, as the account often posts something on Tuesdays at that time. You can scroll through months of posts to see this pattern.

It is so predictable that fans often joke about it in the comments below because they want more GTA 6 info, but instead get posts about GTA Online events or Red Dead Online weekly bonuses. But on the first Thursday following multiple GTA 6 leaks, Rockstar hasn’t posted anything on Twitter. The last post remains a tweet about bonus cash and XP in certain RDO missions.

Shoot your way out of trouble in the Explosive Series, this week’s Red Dead Online Featured Series awarding 3X RDO$ and XP: https://t.co/WCFscxLj2C pic.twitter.com/93DpIM2l8F — Rockstar Games (@RockstarGames) August 18, 2026

Shoot your way out of trouble in the Explosive Series, this week’s Red Dead Online Featured Series awarding 3X RDO$ and XP: https://t.co/WCFscxLj2C pic.twitter.com/93DpIM2l8F

— Rockstar Games (@RockstarGames) August 18, 2026

This complete radio silence extends to Rockstar’s other online accounts, including the studio’s official Instagram account and the company’s Discord server. Over on the official Rockstar Games website, the company hasn’t updated its newswire section at all since August 14.

For the last 48 hours, Rockstar Games has not addressed any of the leaks, nor has it even communicated with fans or press about the situation. Kotaku has pinged Rockstar Games a few times over the last two days and has yet to receive a response.

It isn’t surprising that Rockstar Games has decided to go radio silent right now. The company, as well as Take-Two Interactive, is likely preoccupied with the ongoing GTA 6 gameplay leaks from Cyberleek. The hacker/leaker just shared another clip this morning, this time featuring “leek” being written in bullets on a wall, and is promising to leak even more GTA 6 footage in the near future.

C yberleek has also taunted Rockstar Games by including a clip from a cutscene that features a character claiming to be untraceable due to their use of a VPN.

For Rockstar Games, this is a nightmare situation, and I imagine that posting about RDO or GTA Online events right now isn’t a top priority. Of course, Rockstar is also getting ready to ship the most anticipated game in decades this November. So eventually, it will have to start posting again. But when and what its first message to fans will be following these leaks remains to be seen.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: Hold the throne, NBA 2K27's new MyNBA Legacy mode sounds a lot like basketball Crusader Kings 3
articles.subtitle: Royal court Lo, a new power rose in the East. The warlord Michael of Jordan united the people of Chicago under the crest of the bull, then with his general Scottie of Pippen and the triangular religion of bishop Phil of Jackson, conquered the whole realm.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
Royal court

Lo, a new power rose in the East. The warlord Michael of Jordan united the people of Chicago under the crest of the bull, then with his general Scottie of Pippen and the triangular religion of bishop Phil of Jackson, conquered the whole realm.

Alas, those feeble heirs who inherited Michael's fiefdom upon his passing into retirement failed to retain all he'd won, and soon kings named Kobe of Bryant and LeBron of James vied for supremacy. This, I assume, is how a playthrough of NBA 2K27's new MyNBA Legacy mode might go, given it seems to have taken cues from Crusader Kings 3 's multi-generation dynasty-crafting.

Revealed ahead this week ahead of release on September 4th (there won't be a review of NBA 2K from me this year, at least not right away, as I'm currently busy with a another game), 2K27's bringing some changes and additions to MyNBA. This is the highly-customisable trip through the league's past from the 80s up to the present day which essentially lets you play God and create your own alternate basketball history.

Think the usual manager or player career mode, but with the option to change the past and control the fates of as many teams as you like.

This year, a new variant's been added to this weird mirror universe creator, MyNBA Legacy. "In this all-new player-locked RPG mode, players can take total command of their on-court career while controlling the front office over a 100-year dynasty," reads 2K's explanation of how Legacy differs from their previous offerings.

"Pick any active star, prospect, or Created Player as a Legend and keep their current attributes or revert them to rookie form, then power through stat goals and deep playoff runs to rack up Performance Points.

Players can build an unstoppable multi-generational legacy as descendants inherit their parents' rookie profile as a template, passing down specialised hereditary traits and earning permanent bonuses to fuel Eternal G. O. A. T. status across a 100-year family tree. "

Reckon that sounds a bit Crusader Kings -ish? I do. Pick or create a ruler to step into the shoes of, see how far you can get towards taking over the realm and achieving other goals as them. Then, pick an heir to take on the next leg, hoping that they don't develop or come with all of the worst bits of their ancestors' genetic makeup.

Rather than bemoaning your scaly and sickly sons, you'll be crying because your offspring are just as woeful at free throw shooting as you. 100 years to build a legacy for your dynasty and see how much you can reshape the world according to your whims.

I'm keen to see what it's like, though part of what I typically enjoy about MyNBA is lording over multiple teams rather than concentrating on a single squad or protagonist's story, so I'm not sure all of my 2K27ing will be in Legacy mode.

Then again, maybe surviving yearly West Coast road trips by imagining the Lakers, Warriors, and Clippers are Viking raiders I need to stop from establishing a foothold on the English mainland will prove too alluring. Or, maybe I'll end up playing a Bulls-obssesed Pope in 2K as the perfect prelude to ruling the Papacy in CK3's next expansion.

articles.title: Review: SuperDuper! 4 gets a stem-to-stern revamp, but is just as seaworthy as ever
articles.subtitle: Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper!…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Backups, as any computer user knows, are worth their weight in gold. If it isn’t backed up, it might as well might not exist. That’s why I have for years trusted ShirtPocket’s SuperDuper! to ensure that all my data is safe and sound. And now, for the first time in a very long time, the venerable backup utility has gotten a top-to-bottom update that brings it into the modern era without sacrificing any of the features—and, most importantly, the reliability—that its users have come to depend on.

While SuperDuper! 4 may look like an entirely new beast, its history has stuck around. It still explains what it’s doing in plain English. It still allows you to make complete, bootable backups. It still has its excellent Smart Update option to optimize the copying process.

But it’s gotten some significant updates too. There’s a new interface, for starters, which conforms to Apple’s current Liquid Glass aesthetic, love it or hate it. It’s a bit of a shock to the system after so long without a change, but it’s hard to deny that the old look had grown somewhat antiquated. The result is an app that makes backups as simple and straightforward as they should be, so that anyone can figure it out: click here to set your destination, choose what method, and click Go.

The changes to SuperDuper! 4 also run more than just skin deep. For example, it’s considerably faster than the previous version—up to an order magnitude faster using the new Turbo implementation of Smart Update, according to Shirt Pocket. That’s borne out in my real-world usage. For example, my last nightly backup of 20.55GB took less than 4 minutes.

There are new capabilities here, too. A new Preview feature lets you perform a dry run of your copy job, letting you see every file that will be changed without actually doing any of it. With a new background helper app, copies won’t interrupt whatever you’re doing. And there’s Shortcuts support, so you can run a workflow when your copy job is completed—or even have one of your shortcuts kick off a copy job.

I’ve been using betas of SuperDuper! 4 for a month or so now, and what’s impressed me most is how much it maintains that set-it-and-forget-it strength of the previous versions. The most important thing for a backup is that element of reliability, so when I open up the app and see “31 successful in a row” note, I know that my data is right where it should be.

And if something goes wrong, it’s easier than ever to see what happened: click on a failed job and you’ll get the details, including an Apple Intelligence-powered summary of the job. (You can get that for completed jobs too. )

There are way more features here too, ones that I just don’t have much reason to use for my purposes, but might just well be what you’re looking for. For example, copy rules that let you handle certain files and folders in granular ways, such as excluding certain ones from backups; support for any file system that macOS understands; and there’s support for multiple copy jobs at the same time, even for those that are scheduled.

Backup apps may not be the most exciting software category, but I dare you to find one that’s more crucial. For me, SuperDuper! has done the job for years and I’ve never had any reason to complain about it. Nothing about that seems poised to change with version 4.

SuperDuper! 4 requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later. A free trial version lets you make unlimited full erase backups, but to unlock the rest of the features requires a one-time payment of $43.95. There’s also an upgrade discount for owners of SuperDuper 3 of up to 30 percent. (And, if you bought version 3 very recently, you may be able to get version 4 for free.) And good news: if you need to run backups on older systems, SuperDuper 3 is sticking around.

For everybody who’s already backing up their Macs, SuperDuper! 4 may offer some new features and speed increases that will make the process even smoother. For those of you who aren’t yet…what are you waiting for?

articles.title: SetShot Tracks macOS Settings Changes
articles.subtitle: By now, you’ve probably read “ Decades After HyperCard, AI Is Democratizing Development Again ” (14 August 2026), where I revealed that I used Claude Code to create a full-fledged Mac app called SetShot that takes and compares snapshots of macOS...
articles.author: TidBITS
articles.content:
By now, you’ve probably read “ Decades After HyperCard, AI Is Democratizing Development Again ” (14 August 2026), where I revealed that I used Claude Code to create a full-fledged Mac app called SetShot that takes and compares snapshots of macOS settings.

For a few weeks, SetShot was all I could think about, and I’d wake up in the morning or come home from a bike ride with an idea for a new feature or better interface. Now, and I’m frankly a bit nervous about this, it’s time to show SetShot to the world, although in the time-honored industry hedge, I’m going to claim that it’s still in beta—1. 0b26 as I write this.

The beta state is also my excuse for relying on a GitHub download link —click the SetShot beta link under Assets to download it.

The impetus for SetShot came from helping a friend track down an iPhone connectivity problem that turned out to be related to iCloud Private Relay being enabled during an iOS update (see “ Yet Another Story of an iOS Update Silently Changing Settings,” 10 May 2026).

Similar things have happened in macOS as well, and while iOS sandboxing presents a significant barrier, I wondered if it would be possible to scan the property list (. plist) files Apple uses to store macOS settings.

If that were possible, perhaps I could write something that would take a snapshot of all those settings files, install a macOS update, take another snapshot, and then compare them to see if Apple had silently changed any settings.

Or rather, perhaps Claude Code could write something at my direction. The first step was a proof-of-concept shell script that demonstrated that a script could create and compare snapshots. But since I’m not a command-line guy, I found it awkward to use and difficult to parse the differences—many of which turned out to be random macOS chatter rather than actual settings changes.

That’s when I asked Claude Code to walk me through setting up Xcode for creating a native Swift app that would provide a proper Mac interface. From that initial app, I then spent quite a bit of time over the next month polishing the knowledge base that identifies changes (from over 500 files!

), adding features, pondering and refining the interface, capturing baseline snapshots for clean macOS installs, writing documentation, and prompting ChatGPT repeatedly until I got the icon I wanted.

I’m done, in the sense that I don’t currently have any more ideas for new features or interface changes, and the knowledge base is sufficiently mature to show it to others. So now it’s your turn. If you’re intrigued by the idea of tracking changes to macOS settings—whether they’re made by you or macOS—give it a try. SetShot is free and open source, and it should run on macOS 13 Ventura or later, although I’ve tested it only with macOS 15 Sequoia and macOS 26 Tahoe.

What I enjoyed most was making SetShot into a really good Mac app, with all the behaviors and interface niceties that I’d encourage in apps I review. I’ll call out some of those as I describe SetShot. So, let’s start at the beginning.

SetShot has four views:

Snapshots: Most of your time in SetShot will take place in Snapshots, where you take, select, and compare snapshots.

Journal: The Journal provides a chronological log of all recognized changes across all your comparisons.

Settings: Here you turn on automatic snapshots and adjust their schedule, give permissions that allow SetShot to scan additional settings, change the snapshot sort order, and control software update checking.

About: Full documentation of SetShot’s capabilities lives here. On first launch, SetShot displays the About view to encourage you to read the docs; on all subsequent launches, it defaults to the Snapshots view. It’s searchable, and all the text is selectable.

Snapshots

While developing and testing SetShot, I would take a snapshot, change one or more settings, capture another snapshot, and compare them to see if it recognized my changes. Initially, I started with an interface that listed all the snapshots in two columns, one for Before and one for After, but that ran into some awkwardness when changing the selection.

Formerly indie developer Jason Weingardt, on Threads:

Some personal news: I’ve joined the team at Major League Baseball, and the Mosaic app has come with me. The last 3+ months have, without question, been the wildest of my life.

I’m beyond thankful to MLB for the chance to help shape how fans experience baseball, and even more thankful to the community of fans around the world who tried Mosaic, filed bug reports and feature requests, and helped shape it along the way. We believe Mosaic can be a valuable tool to help learn more about what fans want…. I will keep working on Mosaic as part of my job….

Most importantly: Mosaic is sticking around. Features may come and go, but my ask is that you continue to write in with your feedback about what you like, don’t like, and what you’d want to see in a baseball app. I’m excited for what’s next, and I hope you are too.

Mosaic is a baseball app that’s been in TestFlight for a few months. (Scroll back through Weingardt’s Threads history for details. ) From the moment I saw it, I was dazzled—it’s a great iOS baseball app that uses all of Apple’s platform technologies to lay out live game data and show off other MLB features in ways that MLB’s own app just doesn’t.

And it even integrated with MLB TV, so if you’re a subscriber to MLB’s premium video service, you can watch games via Mosaic, including in the most mind-blowing multiview I’ve seen.

I don’t want to lean too much into the current state of the official MLB app, but it used to be so cutting-edge and great that when I was at Macworld, we gave it a zillion awards and ended up just inducting it into our “app hall of fame.” But over the years, that app has become generic and unfocused and one-size-fits-all. It is no longer a joy to use.

So Jason Weingardt wrote Mosaic, by himself, and it’s a properly great iOS app (that also runs on iPad and Mac and, as of today, Apple TV). I ran into Weingardt at WWDC and he was so happy that people had already fallen in love with his own personal semi-secret passion project.

We all pretty much expected Mosaic to be crushed by MLB once it figured out what was going on. No matter that it was using public APIs and honoring MLB’s own premium content subscriptions, it just felt like the kind of thing that was too good to be true.

Instead, to their immense credit, MLB hired Weingardt, and Mosaic is now apparently a part of MLB’s digital strategy. I almost can’t believe it. It’s the best possible outcome for Weingardt, MLB, and baseball fans with Apple devices.

I’m so happy to think that MLB’s apps may now be on a trajectory to go back to where they belong—in the app hall of fame.

articles.title: Wispr Flow takes on AI meeting assistants with Notetaker, its first product beyond dictation
articles.subtitle: Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: TerminalWidget makes custom widget building easy
articles.subtitle: A TerminalWidget shortcut action and its output. I’m a huge fan of displaying ambient information in my computer interfaces, which on my Mac tends to involve putting data about weather, solar power and the like in my menu bar, so it’s available at a...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’m a huge fan of displaying ambient information in my computer interfaces, which on my Mac tends to involve putting data about weather, solar power and the like in my menu bar, so it’s available at a glance. My tool of choice for this is SwiftBar, itself a follow-on to BitBar (which has been rebooted as xbar ). On my iPad, I’ve been using custom widgets generated with Simon Støvring’s Scriptable app to do the job.

Now here’s a new contender that generates widgets on both Mac and iOS: Brett Terpstra’s $20 TerminalWidget, which lets you send data to a widget from a command-line script, Shortcut, AppleScript, or a URL scheme.

Widgets are more complicated than little items that live in the menu bar. That’s why Scriptable uses little JavaScript scripts to build them. TerminalWidget has a basic set of terminology that lets you target specific widgets and provides some pre-filled functionality that lets you generate some design elements without much hassle. It’ll also just… take text you give it and display it if you want.

If you’re working via Shortcuts, you can update TerminalWidget using a bunch of different template types: Chart, Image, Progress, Table, or Text. Just as with the command line, each Shortcuts action contains a bunch of variables, so you can customize colors and fonts, add a caption and title, or other things that help fill out TerminalWidget’s templates.

It’s by design a lot less flexible than something like Scriptable, where the sky’s the limit—but it’s also a lot more approachable, since you’re basically filling in the blanks with whatever data you want to provide.

I wasn’t really able to replicate my beloved Scriptable weather widget in TerminalWidget—not flexible enough—but TerminalWidget also supports straight-up image use, which allowed me to generate the contents of my Scriptable widget via script, output it as an image, and then tell TerminalWidget to load that image. So if you wanted to offload widget duties to your Mac or a remote server, you could do that and just display the image in TerminalWidget.

In a way, TerminalWidget turns its limitation (lack of flexibility) into a strength, because the learning curve is so gentle, especially if you use Shortcuts, which literally shows you every single possible variable you could possibly use, so you can tinker and figure out what you want to display. Dr. Drang is using it for planetary positions, because that tickles his fancy.

If there’s something you’d like to put on a glanceable widget across iPad, iPhone, and Mac, TerminalWidget will let you do it. That’s a beautiful thing. Now I need to figure out what widgets to add to my own devices…

It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.

articles.title: Subnautica 2′s Co-Op Buddy System Update Is Live, And Has The Coolest Chat
articles.subtitle: Patch Notes Subnautica 2 Unknown Worlds After the fuss over the furious fish, the next-most requested feature in Subnautica 2 ‘s early access has been improved co-op options.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Patch Notes Subnautica 2 Unknown Worlds

After the fuss over the furious fish, the next-most requested feature in Subnautica 2 ‘s early access has been improved co-op options. For reasons beyond me, a lot of people seem to want to play this creepy underwater survival game in packs of chatty Kathys, rather than alone and in silence as is only proper. With version 1.

2 of the game rolling out today, developer Unknown Worlds has now made some big improvements in the co-op department, including adding proximity chat, player trading, and the ability to revive your buddies.

Since the May 14 launch of Subnautica 2 into early access, two topics have dominated the player feedback. The first was the lengthy controversy over whether players should be able to harm the fishies (of course not), and the second was demands for better ways to play in co-op.

Unknown Worlds prioritized the former in the first major update, released July 8, with a compromise of making it easier to deter the more infuriatingly aggressive animals, while also reducing their damage. And this all came with promises that version 1. 2 would focus on friendship.

That’s now out as of today, with a trailer and a vlog to explain more.

Creative director Anthony Gallegos takes the lead on 1.2, explaining what’s changed, with the most important new addition being proximity voice chat. The in-game communication has been done in a neat way that feels very in-universe: Up close you can hear other players clearly over your radios, but the farther apart you get, the poorer the audio quality becomes, breaking up and eventually failing altogether.

There are a bunch of rather corny-looking emotes too, which look very early-2000s MMO, although they seem quite redundant with voice chat. More useful is inventory sharing, where you can walk up to a chum and access their backpack, swapping items between yours and theirs, and again, this maintains immersion, requiring both of you to be immediately next to one another rather than letting you magically teleport items.

The last big addition is player revives. If you die outside, rather than immediately reprinting back at your base, a short timer allows other players to swim in and share oxygen with you to bring you back to life. To make more visual sense of what’s going on in larger groups, there are also two new pioneer skins and new suit colors so you can distinguish yourselves.

Outside of co-op, a few other new features are now in the game, including a device called a tracking tag. Basically an in-game version of an Apple AirTag, you can drop one at a particular location, or even put it inside a container you especially don’t want to lose. Carrying one will also improve your black box location when you die, making it easier to find and recover your loot.

Then there are improvements to the UI, including a better way of displaying icons at distance, and all sorts of tweaks and adjustments to flora and fauna. Oh, and there’s a sneaky glimpse of what looks like a pedal-powered underwater vehicle?

We still seem to be a fair way off from an update that will expand on the game’s current storyline, but with 1.1 and 1.2 addressing the loudest concerns of the game’s player base, perhaps Unknown Worlds will feel more ready to pursue this?

Full patch notes

Here are the full patch notes, and I’m sorry for your mouse’s scroll wheel. (Entries preceded by a snorkeling gear icon are player-suggested changes).

Gameplay

🤿Added Cross-Platform Proximity Voice Chat. As players get further away, they become harder to hear. Voice Chat is available as “always on,” “push to talk,” or “always off.”

Tracking Tag added to the game. Can be placed in carryables (like a locker) as a short-range beacon. If present in hand or inventory when reprinting, will increase black box range.

Players can now revive each other before reprinting. Revived players will keep their equipment and regain a small amount of oxygen. Downed players can also choose to immediately reprint and respawn back at their assigned Biobed.
